newsitem.title: UK: Deutsche economist sees no change in German rates.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche economist sees no change in German rates.

text.p: The Bundesbank is unlikely to alter its key interest rates in the short term despite persistent market speculation of higher rates, said the chief economist at Deutsche Bank, Germany's largest bank.

Deutsche's Norbert Walter told Reuters Financial Television in Singapore on Monday that the Bundesbank is reluctant to tighten monetary policy because of the weak domestic economy and low inflation. But he said the weakening of the mark this year played into the hands of the rate rise story.
"Now that there seems to be some calming down of those pressures, I think the Bundesbank is happy not to do anything," Walter said.
The Bundesbank's policy-making central council meets on Thursday for the first time after its four-week summer recess.
Market speculation the German central bank may nudge up short-term interest rates to support a weakening mark rumbled throughout the Bundesbank's four-week break.
The rate rise speculation, however, has in its own right managed to lift the mark from near eight-year lows against the dollar since last week.
Walter said moves by international investors to place greater emphasis on equities instead of bonds was justified.
"Frankly speaking, under the present circumstances, it is very difficult to see the (global) interest rates going much lower," he said.
On European economic and monetary union (EMU), Walter said there were still risks to a timely start to the single currency on the planned start date of January 1, 1999.
This was mainly because of difficulties in both Germany and France in meeting the entry criteria this year aswell as political and public opposition to the project within Germany, he said
"I guess there is still a two-thirds probability for making it (the 1999 start date) and a one-third risk of not making it," Walter told RFTV.
The Deutsche economist said the most likely founders of EMU would be Germany, France, the Benleux, Austria, Ireland, Finland and "most probably" Spain and Portugal too.
If Italy manages to overhaul its costly public pensions system, then the lira may be included as well, he said.
